The Page curve and Page time only depends very weakly on the belt size. In fact, the only significant effect can be seen at very early times of the evaporation. Figure 17(a) shows that for wide belts, the entanglement between the belts and baths starts growing convexly (i.e., $\partial^{2}\Delta s/\partial\tau_{\Sigma}^{2}>0$ ), then enters a period of concave growth (i.e., $\partial^{2}\Delta s/\partial\tau_{\Sigma}^{2}<0$ ) before entering the linear regime.

Generally, we can separate the time-dependence of the Page curve into four different regimes. At times of the order of the thermal scale $\beta$ ( $\sim 0.16$ in figure 17(a)) the entanglement growth increases until it enters a phase of fast growth between $\tau_{\Sigma}\sim O(\beta)$ and $\tau_{\Sigma}\sim O(\chi_{\Sigma})$ . This fast growth depends on the belt size. At time $\tau_{\Sigma}\sim O(\chi_{\Sigma})$ a universal, linear behavior takes over, which is independent of the belt width. The entanglement keeps growing until at the Page time $\tau_{P}$ it saturates and stays constant.

In the following we will explain the region of fast growth and its transition into the region of universal linear growth. To understand the behaviour of the Page curve, first consider a few characteristics of our belt geometries. As can be seen from the metric in eq. (17), points on any of our entangling surfaces are a fixed distance $\chi_{\Sigma}$ from the surface at $\chi=0$ , where the defect is located, i.e., where the bath is coupled to the black hole.2323 23 The proper distance would be $R\chi_{\Sigma}$ in the boundary metric (13). However, the extrinsic curvature of the entangling surfaces which we consider depends on this distance. Similarly, the entangling surfaces with larger $\chi_{\Sigma}$ have a larger regulated volume.

In [101], it was proposed that the growth of entropy $S[\Sigma]$ for an arbitrary entangling surface $\Sigma$ is bound by

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{R}\frac{dS[\Sigma]}{d\tau}=\frac{dS[\Sigma]}{dt}\leq \displaystyle s_{\mathrm{th}}\,v_{\mathrm{ent}}\,A(\Sigma)\,, $$

where $A(\Sigma)$ is the area of the entangling surface $\Sigma$ , as measured by the boundary metric in eq. (17). The thermal entropy density $s_{\mathrm{th}}$ and the entanglement velocity $v_{\mathrm{ent}}$ are region independent constants. The entropy density is given by the black hole entropy (i.e., $\frac{1}{4G_{\text{bulk}}}$ times horizon area) divided by the CFT volume of the spatial slices (again, measured by the metric (17)):

$$ \displaystyle s_{\mathrm{th}}=\frac{1}{4G_{\text{bulk}}}\,\frac{L^{d-1}}{R^{d-1}}. $$

In [101] which primarily considers flat space, $v_{\mathrm{ent}}$ is defined such that eq. (84) is saturated at times just above the thermal scale for sufficiently straight entangling surfaces – this definition is well-defined in the sense that $v_{\mathrm{ent}}$ turns out to be independent of the shape of the entangling surface, provided it is sufficiently straight [102, 103]. In hyperbolic space, $v_{\mathrm{ent}}$ can be similarly defined by demanding that the straight surface $\chi=0$ saturates eq. (84) – we shall justify this choice further below – specifically,

$$ \displaystyle v_{\mathrm{ent}}= \displaystyle\frac{(d-2)^{\frac{d-2}{2}}}{(d-1)^{\frac{d-1}{2}}}\,, $$

obtained by comparison of eq. (84) with the zero-width belt result in eq. (54).

It is clear that (84) cannot be tight at late times for belts of finite width. The reason is that the area factor on the right hand side $A[\chi>0]$ is exponentially large compared to $A[\chi=0]$ , while, as can be seen from figure 17(a), all belts share the same rate of entanglement growth at late times. To more tightly bound the late time behavior of finite width belts, we will therefore need to combine eq. (84) with the monotonicity of mutual information. It will turn out that the optimal bound obtained in this way for finite-width belts uses eq. (84), but always evaluated for the $\chi=0$ surface $\Sigma$ at late times; thus we will find that the $\chi=0$ surface acts as a bottleneck for entanglement growth even for finite width belts.

To see why the surface at $\chi_{\Sigma}=0$ acts as a bottleneck, let us formulate the more refined combined bound now, following closely [101]. To this end, it will be less helpful to consider the entanglement entropy of the bath intervals $\mathbf{R}$ ; instead we will consider their complement $\bar{\mathbf{R}}$ , i.e., belts surrounding the defects, whose entropy is the same as $\mathbf{R}$ since the state of both Rindler patches is pure. Considering $\bar{\mathbf{R}}$ instead of $\mathbf{R}$ is equivalent to looking at the Page curve of the black hole instead of that of the radiation. It is useful to rewrite the entropy displayed in the Page curve as

$$ \displaystyle\Delta S=I[\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{L}:\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{R}](0)-I[\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{L}:\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{R}](\tau), $$

where $I[\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{L}:\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{R}](\tau)=S(\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{L})+S(\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{R})-S(\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{L}\cup\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{R})$ is the mutual information between the regions $\bar{\mathbf{R}}$ in the left ( $L$ ) and right ( $R$ ) CFT at time $\tau$ .

Similar to [101], we now assume that information is only transported with the butterfly velocity $v_{\mathrm{but}}$ or less.2424 24 The butterfly velocity is defined as the spread of the region in which the commutator of an operator $O_{1}(t)$ with $O_{2}(t)$ is bigger than $1$ [104]. For the hyperbolic geometries considered here and the temperature $T=\frac{1}{2\pi R}$ , this velocity is given by [105, 106]

$$ \displaystyle v_{\mathrm{but}}=\frac{1}{d-1}\,. $$

This implies that a belt region $\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}$ at time $\tau^{\prime}$ can be considered a subsystem of the original belt $\bar{\mathbf{R}}$ at $\tau$ if $\frac{\chi_{\Sigma}-\chi_{\Sigma}^{\prime}}{v_{\mathrm{but}}}\geq|\tau-\tau^{\prime}|$ . We can then use monotonicity of mutual information

$$ \displaystyle I[\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{L}:\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{R}](\tau)\geq I[\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{L}:\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{R}](\tau^{\prime})=S[\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{L}](\tau^{\prime})+S[\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{R}](\tau^{\prime})-S[\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{L}\cup\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{R}](\tau^{\prime}). $$

In our setup, we have that the one-sided entropies are time-independent, $S[\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{R/L}](\tau^{\prime})=S[\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{R/L}](0)$ . Using eq. (84) we can then bound $S[\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{L}\cup\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{R}](\tau^{\prime})$ from above

$$ \displaystyle S[\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{L}\cup\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{R}](\tau^{\prime})\leq Rs_{\mathrm{th}}\,v_{\mathrm{ent}}\,A(\partial\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime})\,\tau^{\prime}+S[\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{L}\cup\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{R}](0). $$

Collecting everything, we find a bound on the Page curve of the black hole,

$$ \displaystyle\Delta S[\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{L}\cup\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{R}]\leq Rs_{\mathrm{th}}\,v_{\mathrm{ent}}\,A(\partial\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime})\,\tau^{\prime}+I[\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{L}:\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{R}](0)-I[\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{L}:\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{R}](0)\,. $$

To find a tightest bound this has to be minimized over all choices of $\chi^{\prime}_{\Sigma}$ , see below. For any fixed $\chi^{\prime}_{\Sigma}$ it is sufficient to focus on the case where $\tau^{\prime}<\tau$ , which will always give the smaller bound. The mutual information appearing on the right hand side are evaluated on the initial time slice and can be obtained numerically by using the results of section 3.3.

From eq. (91), it is now easy to see why the entanglement growth becomes universal at late times. Note that eq. (91) is in fact a family of inequalities, parametrized by a choice of regions $\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}$ . The time $\tau^{\prime}$ is chosen such that $\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}$ at $\tau^{\prime}$ is just barely a subsystem of $\bar{\mathbf{R}}$ at $\tau$ , in the sense described below eq. (88). For times before $\tau^{\prime}$ we assume that the mutual information of subregions $\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}$ is allowed to decrease as fast as possible, while still compatible with eq. (84). Since the regions $\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}$ at time $\tau^{\prime}$ are subregions of $\bar{\mathbf{R}}$ at time $\tau$ , their mutual information bounds the mutual information of regions $\bar{\mathbf{R}}$ . We can find a tight bound on the Page curve by minimizing over all choices of $\bar{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}$ , or in other words, by minimizing over all $\chi^{\prime}_{\Sigma}$ with $\tau^{\prime}=\tau-\frac{\chi_{\Sigma}-\chi_{\Sigma}^{\prime}}{v_{\mathrm{but}}}$ . It turns out that, for sufficiently large $\tau$ , the tightest bound is obtained for $\chi_{\Sigma}^{\prime}=0$ , yielding the prescription stated below eq. (86). We thus see from the first term on the right hand side of eq. (91) that this surface acts as a bottle neck for information transfer and thus controls the late time growth of entropy. Matching this behaviour to the late time rate of growth of the exact Page curve provides further justification, a posteriori, for the choice of the entanglement velocity stated in eq. (86).

The bounds found in this way are presented in figure 17(b). We see that a fast growth at early times is allowed by the bounds, before the linear growth phase is entered. Further, as can be seen from the figure, these bounds are fairly loose. It would be interesting to understand how to make them tighter. Note that the blue curve in figure 17(b) behaves qualitatively different than the other curves. The reason is that the early convex onset of the curve is controlled by the thermal scale and thus lasts for roughly $\Delta\tau\sim O(\beta)$ , independent of the belt width. The rescaling in figure 17(b) magnifies the early time behavior of belts with $\chi_{\Sigma}<1$ while it reduces the early time behavior of belts of width $\chi_{\Sigma}<1$ . Thus, while all other curves show the linear entanglement spreading for time scales $\tau\sim O(\chi_{\Sigma})>O(\beta)$ , the behavior of the blue curve is dominated by entanglement spreading through thermalization, since the belt width is of order of the thermalization scale. For the zero-width, it is easily verified, at least numerically, from eq. (51) that $\sqrt{1-r_{*}}\sim\tau$ so that the growth is indeed quadratic by eq. (52). For finite-width belts, plugging eqs. (65) and (66) into eq. (22) shows that early time evolution is equivalent to holding the cutoff at fixed $\zeta$ and shifting the $\xi$ of the entangling surface by $\sim\tau^{2}$ , again leading to quadratic entanglement growth. growth at times below the thermal scale is reminiscent of the ‘pre-local-equilibration growth’ described in [102, 103].

Let us end with a few observations regarding the structure of entanglement spreading in our system. First, we note that the entanglement velocity (86) for Rindler spacetime with hyperbolic spatial slices differs from the analogous velocity $\sqrt{d}(d-2)^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{d}}/[2(d-1)]^{1-\frac{1}{d}}$ in flat space [94] dual to AdS planar black holes. Furthermore, for $d>3$ , the entangling velocity for a CFT on hyperbolic space exceeds the butterfly velocity, eq. (88). Typically, whenever $v_{\mathrm{ent}}>v_{\mathrm{but}}$ , one might worry about contradictions to entanglement monotonicity laws [107, 101] which apply above the thermal scale. However, no immediate contradictions appear in the present case, as we now explain.

For concreteness, let us interpret eq. (54) as describing the entanglement growth in hyperbolic space without defects, specifically, computing the entropy for a region consisting of half-spaces $\chi>0$ on either side of the TFD.2626 26 To be precise, we should multiply eq. (54) by $\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4G_{\text{bulk}}}$ with the factor of $1/2$ due to our focus on just two copies of the entangling surface $\chi=0$ — one on either side of the TFD. This growth saturates eq. (84) with $v_{\mathrm{ent}}>v_{\mathrm{but}}$ in $d>3$ so one might worry that entanglement is spreading faster than the speed $v_{\mathrm{but}}$ permitted by operator commutator growth [104]. Specifically, by applying an analysis similar to the one reviewed around eq. (88) to thermal relative entropies, [107, 101] argue that, for regions and times above the thermal scale, entanglement growth must be bounded by the thermal entropy density $s_{\mathrm{th}}$ times the volume between the entangling surface and a tsunami wavefront propagating with speed $v_{\mathrm{but}}$ away from the entangling surface (in either direction). Said differently, the rate $dS/dt$ of entanglement growth is bounded by $s_{\mathrm{th}}v_{\mathrm{but}}$ times the area of the tsunami wavefront — this is essentially eq. (84) with $v_{\mathrm{but}}$ replacing $v_{\mathrm{ent}}$ and the tsunami wavefront replacing the entangling surface. In flat space, the tsunami wavefront can be typically chosen to propagate in a direction away from the entangling surface such that it shrinks or does not grow in time (e.g., propagating inward from a spherical entangling surface). Thus, for the flat space equivalent of eq. (84) to be saturated, one must require $v_{\mathrm{ent}}<v_{\mathrm{but}}$ . In hyperbolic space however, it is possible for the tsunami wavefront to grow in both directions away from the entangling surface. Indeed, this is precisely what happens for the hyperbolic half-space which has an entangling surface $\chi=0$ of minimal area; within a few thermal times, the tsunami wavefront propagating in either direction grows to an area exponentially large compared to the entangling surface. We thus see that, though the hyperbolic half-space saturates eq. (84) with $v_{\mathrm{ent}}>v_{\mathrm{but}}$ , this does not contradict the bound on entanglement spreading due to the butterfly velocity.

## 5 Extremal horizon in equilibrium with $T=0$ bath

*Figure 18: The Poincare patch models a zero temperature extremal black hole. The brane intersects the CFT Poincaré patch at the origin and infinity.*

Here we turn our attention to extremal black holes. In particular, we consider the same bulk geometry described in section 2, i.e., a backreacting codimension-one brane extending across the spacetime which locally has the geometry of AdSd+1. However, we replace the AdS-Rindler coordinates introduced in eq. (16) with Poincaré coordinates,

$$ ds^{2}=\frac{L^{2}}{z^{2}}\left(dz^{2}-dt^{2}+dx_{1}^{2}+\cdots+dx_{d-1}^{2}\right)\,. $$

Of course, the coordinate singularity at $z\to\infty$ corresponds to an extremal $T=0$ horizon. Figure 18 illustrates the Poincaré patch in our bulk geometry.

For the most part, we will be interested in limit of large tension (i.e., $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\gg L$ ), for which the brane theory can be described as Einstein gravity coupled to two copies of the boundary CFT. As we describe in a moment, the brane geometry naturally inherits a Poincaré metric from the bulk geometry. Hence the brane supports an extremal black hole which is equilibrium with the $T=0$ bath CFT on the asymptotic AdS boundary. We note that with Poincaré coordinates, we are examining the system in a new conformal frame where the bath CFT is living on flat $d$ -dimensional Minkowski space,

$$ ds_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}^{2}=-dt^{2}+dx_{1}^{2}+\cdots+dx_{d-1}^{2}\,. $$

This brane perspective is illustrated in figure 19a.

Of course, we may also have the boundary perspective where the $d$ -dimensional CFT in Minkowski space is coupled to a codimension-one conformal defect. For simplicity, we insert the latter at $x_{1}=0$ for the metric in eq. (93) and so the induced geometry on the defect is also flat, i.e., ( $d$ –1)-dimensional Minkowski space. The Penrose diagram for this perspective is shown in figure 19b. Note that in contrast to the finite temperature TFD state (entangling two copies of the bath CFT) in section 3, here for the $T=0$ scenario, we only have a single copy of the bath CFT, e.g., compare the above to figures 6 and 7. Of course, at $T=0$ , we are simply studying the vacuum state of the defect CFT in flat space (analogous to what was done in [1] but in a different conformal frame).2727 27 Of course, this is a pure state, as is manifest in bulk since the Poincaré time slices constitute complete Cauchy slices.

We may recall from [2] that for the extremal case in $d=2$ , one always finds islands for the analogous belt regions. This result is a consequence of two features which hold for $d=2$ : firstly, there always exists a bulk RT surface intersecting the brane to produce an island; secondly, the alternative no-island RT candidate surface has an additional IR divergence2828 28 Coming from integrating the length of the surface down to the extremal horizon. and this surface is therefore subdominant. However, neither of these statements hold in $d\geq 3$ . Indeed, we will find in higher dimensions that quantum extremal islands do not appear in the large tension limit. Nonetheless, no information paradox arises since extremal black holes do not radiate, i.e., the black hole and the bath are not exchanging radiation. This contrasts with the non-extremal case in section 3, where the information paradox for the eternal black hole in the effective $d$ -dimensional gravity theory arises because of the continuous exchange of quanta between the black hole and the bath. Of course, the paradox is avoided by the appearance of quantum extremal islands.

Specifically, we consider the entanglement entropy calculation for a boundary region $\mathbf{R}$ that is the complement of a “belt” geometry centered on the defect at $x_{1}=0$ , i.e., the boundary subregion $\mathbf{R}=(-\infty,-b]\cup[b,\infty)$ . However, by a simply Weyl transformation, the brane metric becomes flat and further both the intrinsic and the extrinsic curvatures of $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ vanish. Hence in this flat conformal frame, the higher curvature corrections to the Wald-Dong entropy individually vanish. Hence while these curvatures do not vanish in the original conformal frame, the higher curvature entropy corrections must all cancel against one another. Turning to the first term in the first line of eq. (110), we have the area law divergence associated with the two components of the entangling surface $\Sigma_{\mathrm{CFT}}$ at $x_{1}=\pm b$ . This leaves us with the second term in the first line. Upon closer examination can be recognized as the finite contribution to the entanglement entropy for a belt of width $D$ , up to an additional factor of 2, e.g., see [17, 16]. Further, we note that both contributions on the first line of eq. (109) contain a prefactor proportional to $L^{d-1}/G_{\text{bulk}}\sim c_{T}$ , which measures the number of degrees of freedom in the boundary CFT, e.g., [86].

We can see that these results correspond approximately to the expected entropy from the brane perspective as follows: We begin by considering the contribution from the CFT to one side of the conformal defect, say $x_{1}<0$ . Imagine we begin with a single copy of the CFT in flat space (93), and evaluate the entropy of a belt of width $D$ with entangling surfaces at $x_{1}=-b$ and $x_{1}=D-b$ . For this geometry, the holographic entanglement entropy becomes [17, 16]

$$ S_{\textrm{\tiny EE}}=\frac{L^{d-1}}{4G_{\text{bulk}}}\Bigg\{\frac{1}{d-2}\frac{\mathrm{vol}_{d-2}^{\perp}}{\delta^{d-2}}+\frac{1}{d-2}\frac{\mathrm{vol}_{d-2}^{\perp}}{\delta^{d-2}}-\frac{1}{d-2}\left(\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma\!\left[\frac{d}{2(d-1)}\right]}{(d-2)\,\Gamma\!\left[\frac{1}{2(d-1)}\right]}\right)^{d-1}\frac{\mathrm{vol}_{d-2}^{\perp}}{D^{d-2}}\Bigg\}\,, $$

where we have separated the area law contributions of the two components of the entangling surface. Now from the brane perspective in our system, the bath CFT reside in flat space for $x_{1}<0$ but the corresponding copy of the CFT resides onto the AdSd geometry of the brane for $x_{1}>0$ . However the latter can be produced by making a local Weyl transformation in the positive $x_{1}$ domain:

$$ ds^{2}=\frac{\delta^{2}}{x_{1}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}\,ds_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}^{2}=\frac{\delta^{2}}{x_{1}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}\left(-dt^{2}+dx_{1}^{2}+\cdots+dx_{d-1}^{2}\right)\,. $$

Note that this is geometry is not the induced metric (96) but rather we are considering the standard conformal frame where one strips off the factor of $(L/\delta)^{2}$ from the bulk metric.3232 32 Further, we are only performing the Weyl transformation (112) for $x_{1}>\delta/\tan\theta_{B}$ , which corresponds to the intersection of the brane with the UV cutoff surface $z=\delta$ . Now the net effect of this Weyl transformation on the entanglement entropy (111) is to modify the cutoff appearing in the area law contribution for the surface at $x_{1}=D-b$ , i.e., $\delta\to(D-b)\sin\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\simeq z_{\mathrm{QES}}$ , where the latter assumes that $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\ll 1$ . Hence the entropy (111) becomes

$$ \displaystyle S^{\prime}_{\textrm{\tiny EE}} \displaystyle\simeq \displaystyle\frac{L^{d-1}}{4G_{\text{bulk}}}\Bigg\{\frac{1}{d-2}\frac{\mathrm{vol}_{d-2}^{\perp}}{\delta^{d-2}}-\frac{1}{d-2}\left(\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma\!\left[\frac{d}{2(d-1)}\right]}{(d-2)\,\Gamma\!\left[\frac{1}{2(d-1)}\right]}\right)^{d-1}\frac{\mathrm{vol}_{d-2}^{\perp}}{D^{d-2}}\Bigg\} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\frac{1}{4}\,\frac{L}{(d-2)G_{\text{bulk}}}\left(\frac{L}{z_{\mathrm{QES}}}\right)^{d-2}\frac{\mathrm{vol}_{d-2}^{\perp}}{\delta^{d-2}}\,. $$

Now using eq. (9), the term on the second line can be recognized as the contribution of one of the boundary CFTs to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of the quantum extremal surface on the brane. Hence combining the above contribution (113) with that from the other copy of the boundary CFT (which extends to the bath for $x_{1}>0$ ) and the DGP contribution to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, we precisely recover the leading contributions in eq. (110). Hence this simple CFT argument allows us to match the leading contributions in the holographic result with the expected entanglement entropy.

### 5.2 No-island phase

Above, we studied the set of candidate RT surfaces which intersect the brane. In fact (for $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}<\pi/2$ ), there exists another set of simple extremal surfaces which must also be considered under the RT prescription (2). These surfaces are constant $x_{1}$ planes anchored on the entangling surface $\Sigma_{\mathrm{CFT}}$ on the asymptotic boundary and fall straight into the bulk. By reflection symmetry about $x_{1}=\pm b$ , these planes trivially extremize the area functional, which becomes

$$ A(\mathbf{V})=2L^{d-1}\mathrm{vol}_{d-2}^{\perp}\int_{\mathbf{V}}\frac{dz}{z^{d-1}}\,. $$

A factor of $2$ has been included above to account for the two planes at $x_{1}=\pm b$ .3333 33 Further, let us note that for the special case $d=2$ , the integral produces an IR divergence at $z\to\infty$ . However, there is no such IR divergence for $d\geq 3$ . Unlike the surfaces considered in section 5.1, these planes do not intersect the brane and thus no islands are formed on the brane. The entropy in this no-island phase is easily obtained from evaluating the area functional (114), which then yields

$$ \displaystyle\frac{A(\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\text{bulk}}}= \displaystyle\frac{L^{d-1}}{2(d-2)G_{\text{bulk}}}\,\frac{\mathrm{vol}_{d-2}^{\perp}}{\delta^{d-2}}\,, $$

where $\delta$ is again the UV cutoff in the boundary CFT.

### 5.3 Islands at $T=0$ for $d>2$

Altogether, we have two candidate RT surfaces: the extremal surfaces described in section 5.1 which intersect the brane to form a quantum extremal island, and the extremal planes described in section 5.2 corresponding to the no-island phase. To determine which is the correct RT surface, we must first study the parameter space for which each surface exists. When both types surfaces exist simultaneously, the correct RT surface is given by the one which has the smallest generalized entropy, as in eq. (2). Below, we first observe that on a brane at angle $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}<\pi/2$ , an island can only possibly exist when $-1<\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}<1$ ; more specifically, for this range of the DGP parameter $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}$ , there is a critical angle $\theta_{c}<\pi/2$ which gives the minimum $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ that supports the island phase – recall that this critical angle was plotted in figure 22(b). For $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}>\theta_{c}$ , the island phase exists and is dominant. At $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}=\theta_{c}$ the entropies computed by the island and no-island RT surfaces equalize, leading to a transition to the no-island phase below $\theta_{c}$ . As we shall find that $\theta_{c}$ scales as $(1+\lambda_{b})^{\frac{1}{d-2}}$ at its smallest, this precludes the possibility of islands in the regime where the brane is well-described by QFT on semiclassical gravity – see footnote 5. This differs from the $d=2$ case, where the island phase always exists; furthermore, while the no-island RT surface in $d>3$ has an IR-finite area, the analogous surfaces in $d=2$ produce an IR divergence and thus are never dominant.

Let us begin our analysis by constraining the parameter space in which each type of RT candidate surface exists. It is easy to see that the extremal planes of the no-island phase exist if and only if $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\leq\pi/2$ .3434 34 Of course, this was our regime of interest, as this was the regime where a (nearly) massless graviton is induced on the brane. It is slightly more involved to determine when the extremal surfaces in the island phase exists. For a start, the first equality of eq. (106) indicates that for $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}<\pi/2$ , sensible extremal surfaces intersecting the brane can only possibly exist when $-1<\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}<1$ .3535 35 Specifically, this can be seen as follows: Let us take the extreme case of $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}=1$ ( $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}=-1$ ). Then eq. (106) indicates that $\theta_{\mathrm{QES}}=\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}-\pi/2$ ( $\theta_{\mathrm{QES}}=\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}+\pi/2$ ). For $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}=1$ , this implies that when $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}>\pi/2$ , the RT surface falls straight into the bulk until it hits the brane, i.e., $z_{*}=\infty$ – see figure 20. Now as $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\to\pi/2$ from above, the QES runs off towards the horizon and consequently no QES exists for $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}<\pi/2$ . For $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}=-1$ , one can argue that for $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}<\pi/2$ , the QES is stuck to the defect, i.e., $z_{\mathrm{QES}}=\infty$ . As increasing (decreasing) $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}$ beyond $1$ ( $-1$ ) means the DGP entropy contribution exerts a greater force pushing the QES towards the horizon (the defect), it follows that no QES exists for $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}<\pi/2$ when $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}>1$ ( $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}<-1$ ). In these parameter ranges, the naive ‘solutions’ obtained from eq. (106) are unphysical, i.e., have the RT surface anchored in the unphysical region behind the brane. From figure 22(a), we see that this is the range of $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}$ for which there exists some $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}<\pi/2$ such that the DGP gradient has not overpowered the bulk term of eq. (105) to push the QES to the asymptotic boundary $y=0$ or to the horizon $y=\infty$ .

To be more precise, we must consider properties of the $\mathcal{F}$ function introduced in eq. (108). For $-1<\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}<1$ , some (numerically deduced) facts about $\mathcal{F}(d,\lambda_{\mathrm{b}},\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}})$ are that it is decreasing in $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}$ and increasing in $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ . Moreover,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{F}(d,\lambda_{\mathrm{b}},\text{$\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ close to $0$})={} \displaystyle-(1+\lambda_{\mathrm{b}})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{-\frac{d-2}{d-1}}[1+O(\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2})]+\frac{D}{z_{*}} \displaystyle\mathcal{F}(d,\lambda_{\mathrm{b}},\text{$\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ close to $\pi$})={} \displaystyle(1-\lambda_{\mathrm{b}})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}(\pi-\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}})^{-\frac{d-2}{d-1}}\{1+O[(\pi-\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}})^{2}]\}. $$

Since the former diverges negatively while the latter diverges positively, it follows that there exists a critical angle $\theta_{c}$ for which $\mathcal{F}(d,\lambda_{\mathrm{b}},\theta_{c})=0$ . For $-1<\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}<1$ , we have $0<\theta_{c}<\pi/2$ with $\theta_{c}\to 0,\pi/2$ as $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}\to-1,1$ , respectively.3636 36 In particular then, no islands form with $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}>1$ in the regime of interest with $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\leq\pi/2$ . The physical significance of $\theta_{c}$ can be seen from the second equality of eq. (107): for $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ above $\theta_{c}$ , there exist extremal surfaces which intersect the brane; as $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\to\theta_{c}$ from above, $z_{*},z_{\mathrm{QES}},y_{\mathrm{QES}}$ run off to $+\infty$ as $\sim(\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}-\theta_{c})^{-1}$ ; finally, for $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}<\theta_{c}$ , no extremal surfaces exist which intersect the brane. In Figure 22(b), we plot the critical angle $\theta_{c}$ as a function of $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}$ for various $d$ .

Before continuing, let us briefly note a number of peculiarities which arise when $|\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}|>1$ . First, for $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}>1$ , there exists a range of $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\gtrsim\pi/2$ for which no extremal surfaces of any kind exists, i.e., the RT prescription fails completely. This may indicate that there is no CFT plus defect theory which can be dual to a bulk with this range of parameters – of course, the brane has a negative tension in this regime and so there is no effective gravitational theory on the brane. Second, recall that as $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}\to-1$ from above, the coefficient of the Einstein-Hilbert action vanishes, leading to a breakdown of semiclassical Einstein gravity, as mentioned in footnote 5. Further taking $\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}<-1$ then corresponds leads to an unphysical ghost-like gravity action in the brane theory. At any rate, from here on, we shall restrict our focus to $-1<\lambda_{\mathrm{b}}<1$ .

Now we have two competing possible RT surfaces: for $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\leq\pi/2$ , extremal planes anchored on the entangling surfaces to either side of the brane, which correspond to a no-island phase; and, for $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}>\theta_{c}$ , extremal surfaces which intersect the brane, corresponding to an island phase. As both types of surfaces exist for $\theta_{c}<\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}<\pi/2$ , the RT formula instructs us to choose the surface with the smallest area in this parameter space. We briefly comment that, unlike for the CFT region considered in [1], the addition of topological terms to the bulk gravity theory does not change the favourability between the island and no-island phases of the belt geometry. This is because such a modification can only effect a topological contribution to the Wald-Dong entropy formula and, for the belt geometry, the RT surfaces in both phases have vanishing Euler characteristic. Namely, the RT surface of the island phase has the topology of an infinite strip while the RT surface of the no-island phase consists of two half-planes. Thus, the topological contribution would not favour one phase over the other.

In closing, we note that, unlike the $d=2$ case [2], we have found that in the small $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ limit, where an effective theory of gravity plus quantum matter emerges on the brane, islands typically do not exist for extremal black holes in $d\geq 3$ . We remark that, unlike for non-extremal black holes to be discussed in section 3, there is no immediate information paradox that arises as a result of the lack of islands in the extremal case here.

## 6 Two dimensions revisited

In this section, we specialize to the case of $d=2$ which, as mentioned in the main text, requires a slightly different treatment. We begin with a discussion of the induced action on the brane, supplemented with JT gravity. Next, we review the bulk AdS3 and brane AdS2 geometries. Finally, we study extremal surfaces serving as candidate RT surfaces to determine the entropy in the two phases, with and without an island, leading to the Page curve. At leading order in an expansion in terms of small brane angles, i.e., $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\to 0$ , our results precisely agree to those of [2]. However, we can also retain the subleading terms, which produce corrections due to the finite UV cutoff on the brane.

### 6.1 Brane action

We begin by briefly reviewing the modifications for the induced brane action in two dimensions – a more complete discussion can be found in [1].

Let us start in the absence of JT gravity, considering only the brane action $I_{\mathrm{induced}}$ induced by the bulk Einstein-Hilbert action (with cosmological constant) given in eq. (3), its corresponding Gibbons-Hawking action on the brane, and the brane tension term

$$ \displaystyle I_{\mathrm{brane}}= \displaystyle-T_{o}\int d^{2}x\;\sqrt{-\tilde{g}}. $$

As we saw in section 2, the induced action evaluated for higher dimensions contains coefficients with factors of $(d-2)$ (see eq. (8)), which prevent a naive substitution $d\to 2$ . Instead, redoing the calculation specifically in two dimensions, the induced brane action is found to be

$$ I_{\textrm{\tiny induced}}=\frac{1}{16\pi G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}\int d^{2}x\sqrt{-\tilde{g}}\Big[\frac{2}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}^{2}}-\tilde{R}\,\log\left(-\frac{L^{2}}{2}{\tilde{R}}\right)+{\tilde{R}}+\frac{L^{2}}{8}\,\tilde{R}^{2}+\cdots\Big]\,. $$

where the two effective scales are

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{L}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}\right)^{2}= \displaystyle 2\left(1-4\pi G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}LT_{o}\right)\;, \displaystyle G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}= \displaystyle G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}/L\,. $$

Notice that while the first equality follows the same definition as in higher dimensions, the second one must be redefined for $d=2$ (c.f. eq. (9)). The unusual logarithmic term above arises from the nonlocal Polyakov action [110], which appears from integrating out the two-dimensional CFT on the brane – see the discussion in [1]. In the absence of any DGP terms in the brane, extremization of $I_{\mathrm{induced}}$ leads to an $\mathrm{AdS}_{2}$ brane with radius of curvature $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ related to $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}$ in the same way as in higher dimensions (i.e., through eqs. (6) and (9)):

$$ \frac{L^{2}}{{\ell}_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}^{2}}=f\!\left(\frac{L^{2}}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}\right)\equiv 2\left(1-\sqrt{1-\frac{L^{2}}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}}\,\right)\,. $$

Thus, as in the higher dimensional case, the large tension limit leads to $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\gg L$ and a small brane angle $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ in eq. (6). In this limit, the brane moves towards the would-be $\mathrm{AdS}_{3}$ boundary at $\theta=0$ , giving rise to a logarithmic UV divergence in eq. (122) as $L/\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\to 0$ .

Throughout the main text, we considered supplementing the brane action with a DGP term — compare eqs. (4) and (121). In two dimensions, an Einstein-Hilbert action is topological and so it is common to instead consider Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity [111, 112] in the brane theory (e.g., see recent discussions of quantum extremal islands in $d=2$ , e.g., [13, 15, 2, 113]). Following [1], we then choose the brane action as

$$ I_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}=I_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}-\frac{1}{4\pi G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}L}\int d^{2}x\sqrt{-\tilde{g}}\,, $$

with the JT action taking the usual form (again as in section 2, we are omitting boundary terms),

$$ I_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}=\frac{1}{16\pi G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\int d^{2}x\sqrt{-\tilde{g}}\left[\Phi_{0}\,\tilde{R}+\Phi\left(\tilde{R}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}}\right)\right]\,. $$

The Einstein-Hilbert term, though topological, still contributes to the generalized entropy with weight $\Phi_{0}$ . With the addition of JT gravity on the brane in eq. (125), we arrive at the following induced action on the brane,

$$ \displaystyle I_{\textrm{\tiny induced}}=\frac{1}{16\pi G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}\int d^{2}x\sqrt{-\tilde{g}}\Big[-\tilde{R}\,\log\left(-\frac{L^{2}}{2}{\tilde{R}}\right)+\frac{L^{2}}{8}\,\tilde{R}^{2}+\cdots\Big] \displaystyle\qquad+\frac{1}{16\pi G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\int d^{2}x\sqrt{-\tilde{g}}\left[\tilde{\Phi}_{0}\,\tilde{R}+\Phi\left(\tilde{R}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}}\right)\right]\,, $$

where we have redefined the topological part of the dilaton upon collecting the coefficients multiplying an Einstein-Hilbert terms, i.e.,

$$ \tilde{\Phi}_{0}=\Phi_{0}+G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}/G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}\,. $$

Note that we have discarded the usual tension coefficient $T_{o}$ in eq. (125) and instead chosen the tension such that no cosmological constant appears in the first line of eq. (127) for simplicity. In eq. (127), it is clear that varying $\Phi$ yields an equation of motion simply setting the radius of curvature on the brane to $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}=\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}$ . The limit of small brane angle $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ , related to $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ still through the first equality of eq. (6), is therefore obtained by taking $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}\ll L$ . Note that this leads to a logarithmic UV divergence in eq. (127) similar to the non-JT case, as mentioned below eq. (124). Similarly, the source-free equations of motion for the dilaton can then be obtained by varying the metric and further shifting the dilaton, as discussed in [1].

The above reviews our discussion of the induced action in [1]. However, we would like to compare our results for the quantum extremal surfaces and the Page curve to those derived in [2]. To facilitate this comparison, we make the following field redefinitions

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{0}= \displaystyle\ \frac{\Phi_{0}}{4G_{\mathrm{brane}}}\,, \displaystyle\phi= \displaystyle\ \phi_{0}+\frac{\Phi}{4G_{\mathrm{brane}}}\,, \displaystyle\tilde{\phi}_{0}= \displaystyle\ \phi_{0}-\frac{1}{2G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}\log\left(\frac{L}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}}\right)\,, \displaystyle\tilde{\phi}= \displaystyle\ \phi-\frac{1}{2G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}\log\left(\frac{L}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}}\right), $$

giving the bare and renormalized values of the dilaton — we shall clarify the meaning of this renormalization shortly. In terms of the latter, induced action (127) now reads

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}I_{\mathrm{induced}}=&\frac{1}{16\pi G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}\int d^{2}x\;\sqrt{-\tilde{g}}\left[-\tilde{R}\,\log\left(-\frac{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}^{2}}{2}{\tilde{R}}\right)+\tilde{R}+\frac{L^{2}}{8}\,\tilde{R}^{2}+\cdots\right]\\
&+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int d^{2}x\;\sqrt{-\tilde{g}}\left[\tilde{\phi}\,\tilde{R}+\frac{2}{\ell^{2}_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}}(\tilde{\phi}-\tilde{\phi}_{0})\right]\,.\end{split} $$

Here, the first line eq. (131) may be interpreted as the renormalized effective action produced by integating out the brane CFT, and the second line contains the renormalized JT action, which can be compared to eq. (2) in [2]. Here, ‘renormalized’ means that we have absorbed the logarithmic UV divergence that would otherwise appear in the induced action3838 38 Recall that we also removed the power law divergence corresponding to the induced cosmological constant term by introducing a counterterm in eq. (125). as $L/\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\to 0$ into the JT action, which was achieved by the renormalization of $\phi_{0}\to\tilde{\phi}_{0}$ in eq. (130).

As before, the dilaton $\tilde{\phi}$ acts as a Lagrange multiplier which fixes the brane geometry to be locally $\mathrm{AdS}_{2}$ with radius of curvature $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}=\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}$ . The equation of motion for the induced metric $\tilde{g}_{ij}$ , on the other hand, yields the dilaton equation of motion

$$ -\nabla_{i}\nabla_{j}\tilde{\phi}+\tilde{g}_{ij}\left(\nabla^{2}\tilde{\phi}-\frac{\tilde{\phi}-\tilde{\phi}_{0}}{\ell^{2}_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}}\right)=2\pi\,\widetilde{T}^{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}_{ij}=-\frac{\tilde{g}_{ij}}{4L^{2}G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}\,f\!\left(\frac{L^{2}}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}^{2}}\right)\,. $$

In the final expression, we evaluated the renormalized CFT stress tensor $\widetilde{T}^{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}_{ij}$ using the function $f$ defined in eq. (124).3939 39 As noted in [1], $f(L^{2}/\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}^{2})=L^{2}/\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}^{2}+O(L^{4}/\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}^{4})$ and hence this expression yields the expected trace anomaly $\langle(\widetilde{T}^{\textrm{\tiny CFT}})^{i}{}_{i}\rangle=2\times\frac{c}{24\pi}\,\tilde{R}$ to leading order in $L/\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}$ . But the latter also receives additional corrections due to the finite UV cutoff on the brane – see eq. (2.45) in [1]. Recall that the central charge of the boundary CFT is given by $c={3L}/{2G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}$ and the extra factor of two in the trace anomaly arises because the brane supports two copies of this CFT. The standard discussions of JT gravity (e.g., [114, 13]) refer to the source-free dilaton equation, i.e., the RHS vanishes, but this is easily accommodated by a further shift4040 40 Note that implementing this shift in the action (131) introduces a new cosmological constant term. Hence an alternative approach would be to introduce a general brane tension $T_{o}$ in eq. (125) and then tune the latter to absorb both the corresponding (power law) UV divergence in the induced action and the RHS of the dilaton equation (132).

$$ \hat{\phi}_{0}=\tilde{\phi}_{0}+\frac{\ell^{2}_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}}{4L^{2}G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}\,f\!\left(\frac{L^{2}}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}^{2}}\right)\,. $$

### 6.2 Bulk and brane geometries

Let us now review the geometry for our current setup. Due to the simplicity of AdS3, we will find it convenient to describe RT surfaces using global coordinates, even though we will be considering Rindler time evolution, as in the main text. In global coordinates, we may write the bulk $\mathrm{AdS}_{3}$ metric as

$$ \displaystyle ds^{2}=\frac{L^{2}}{\cos^{2}\tilde{r}}\left[-d\tilde{\tau}^{2}+d\tilde{r}^{2}+\sin^{2}\tilde{r}\,d\varphi^{2}\right] $$

where $\tilde{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}$ , $\tilde{r}\in[0,\pi/2]$ and $\varphi\in[-\pi,\pi]$ .

In the AdS-Rindler coordinates, the AdS3 geometry becomes

$$ \displaystyle ds^{2} \displaystyle=L^{2}\left(-(r^{2}-1)\,d\tau^{2}+\frac{dr^{2}}{r^{2}-1}+r^{2}d\chi^{2}\right)\,, $$

which is just the special case of eq. (16) for $d$ =2. Here, $\tau,\chi\in(-\infty,\infty)$ and one exterior region is given by $r>1$ . As described in section 2, the AdS-Rindler coordinates are useful for the description of vacuum AdS as a topological black hole, such that the boundary CFT is in a thermofield double state. The inverse temperature with respect to time $\tau$ is $2\pi$ , giving the periodicity of $i\tau$ necessary for a smooth Euclidean continuation — we shall also define a dimensionful time and temperature shortly. Indeed, these coordinates describe a horizon at $r=1$ . Note that in $d=2$ , the boundary geometry is flat, i.e., it is simply two copies of ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ . The AdS-Rindler coordinates $(\tau,r,\chi)$ are related to the global coordinates $(\tilde{\tau},\tilde{r},\varphi)$ in eq. (134) by

$$ \displaystyle\tanh\tau= \displaystyle\frac{\sin\tilde{\tau}}{\cos\varphi\,\sin\tilde{r}}\,, \displaystyle\tanh\chi= \displaystyle\frac{\sin\varphi\,\sin\tilde{r}}{\cos\tilde{\tau}}\,, \displaystyle r^{2}= \displaystyle\frac{\cos^{2}\tilde{\tau}-\sin^{2}\varphi\,\sin^{2}\tilde{r}}{\cos^{2}\tilde{r}}\,. $$

As described above in section 6.1, extremizing the brane action in eq. (127) with respect to $\Phi$ (or eq. (131) with respect to $\tilde{\phi}$ ) fixes the intrinsic brane geometry to be $\mathrm{AdS}_{2}$ with radius of curvature $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}=\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}$ . This becomes the $\theta=\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ slice of the AdS3 metric written as in eq. (5), where $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ is determined by

$$ \sin\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}=\frac{L}{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}}\,, $$

as in eq. (18). We write the induced metric on the brane as

$$ \ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}^{2}ds_{\mathrm{AdS}_{2}}^{2}=\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}^{2}\left(-(\rho^{2}-1)\,d\tau^{2}+\frac{d\rho^{2}}{\rho^{2}-1}\right)=-\frac{4\pi^{2}\,\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}^{2}}{\beta^{2}}\,\frac{dy^{+}dy^{-}}{\sinh^{2}\!\left(\frac{\pi(y^{+}-y^{-})}{\beta}\right)}\,. $$

The first line element with $(\tau,\rho)$ is simply the special case of AdS-Rindler coordinates given in eq. (20) with $d=2$ . The light-cone coordinates $(y^{+},y^{-})$ in the second line element are those used by [2], whose results we wish to compare against. The relationship between $(\tau,\rho)$ and $(y^{+},y^{-})$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\tau= \displaystyle\frac{\pi(y^{+}+y^{-})}{\beta}=\frac{2\pi t}{\beta}\,, \displaystyle\rho= \displaystyle\coth\left[\frac{\pi(y^{+}-y^{-})}{\beta}\right]. $$

Given that the TFD has temperature $\frac{1}{2\pi}$ with respect to dimensionless time $\tau$ , we have introduced the dimensionful time $t=\frac{y^{+}+y^{-}}{2}$ where the temperature becomes $T=1/\beta$ .4141 41 This is the same time coordinate introduced below eq. (16), though the relation $\beta=2\pi\,R$ loses its meaning as there is no spatial curvature in $d=2$ .

On the brane, eq. (132) is easily solved for the dilaton profile in terms of $\rho$ or $y^{\pm}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\phi} \displaystyle=\hat{\phi}_{0}+\frac{2\pi\phi_{r}}{\beta}\,\rho=\hat{\phi}_{0}+\frac{2\pi\phi_{r}}{\beta}\,\coth\!\left[\frac{\pi(y^{+}-y^{-})}{\beta}\right]\,, $$

where $\phi_{r}$ is a constant introduced in [2] (see eq. (18) and discussion below (2) there).

In the AdS-Rindler metric given in eq. (135), we introduce a surface of large constant $r=r_{\mathrm{UV}}$ which will serve as the UV cutoff surface. Then following [2], we take the induced metric on this surface as the background metric for the bath CFT, i.e.,

$$ ds^{2}_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}=L^{2}r_{\mathrm{UV}}^{2}(-d\tau^{2}+d\chi^{2})\,, $$

with the conformal defect at $\chi=0$ . Now the light-cone coordinates $y^{\pm}$ can be extended to describe the geometry of $\mathrm{AdS}_{3}$ bulk, and in particular the bath region on the asymptotic boundary near $\theta=\pi$ as well as the brane geometry given in eq. (138) at $\theta=\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ , by taking an AdS3 metric in the form eq. (5). Indeed, on the asymptotic boundary, with metric given in eq. (141), $y^{\pm}$ are related to $(\tau,\chi)$ with4242 42 We should note that the geometry in [2] can be seen as a ${\mathbb{Z}}_{2}$ orbifold of our setup (see section 2.2). Hence they would only consider $\chi<0$ of the flat boundary geometry in eq. (141). Therefore, the extension of the null coordinates that we are discussing here has to be considered separately for each side of the conformal defect. As a technical point, let us add that in [2], the sign of the spatial coordinate on the brane is reversed so that $y^{+}-y^{-}>0$ describes the asymptotic boundary while $y^{+}-y^{-}<0$ describes the brane. Here, $y^{+}-y^{-}$ is always positive and $\theta=\pi,\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ correspond respectively to the bath and brane.

$$ \displaystyle y^{\pm}= \displaystyle\frac{\beta(\tau\mp\chi)}{2\pi}\,, \displaystyle ds^{2}_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}= \displaystyle-\left(\frac{2\pi Lr_{\mathrm{UV}}}{\beta}\right)^{2}dy^{+}dy^{-}\,. $$

As in higher dimensions, we are interested in computing the entanglement entropy of a boundary region $\mathbf{R}$ comprised of all of the points with $|\chi|\geq\chi_{\Sigma}$ in the two baths (associated with the two copies of the CFT entangled in the TFD state). That is, this region is the complement of two intervals (‘belts’) centered on the conformal defects in the two boundaries (which corresponds to the intersection of the brane with the asymptotic boundary – see figure 23). Focusing on a single Rindler wedge and on one side of the brane, the entangling surface is located at a fixed $\chi=-\chi_{\Sigma}<0$ , which we define as

$$ \frac{y^{+}-y^{-}}{2}=b>0\qquad{\rm with}\quad b=\frac{\beta}{2\pi}\,\chi_{\Sigma}\,, $$

for all Rindler times $\tau$ . Similar assignments apply for the patches covering the other portions of the boundary.

Finally, we note that going to the asymptotic boundary (with $\tilde{r}\to\pi/2$ and $r\to\infty$ ), eq. (136) yields the relation of the global and Rindler coordinates on the boundary:

$$ \displaystyle\tan\varphi \displaystyle=\frac{\sinh\chi}{\cosh\tau}\ \ \ ,\ \ \ \tan\tilde{\tau}=\frac{\sinh\tau}{\cosh\chi}\ , $$

which allow us to simplify some calculations below. It will be useful to denote the (time-dependent) global coordinate angle of the entangling surface at $\chi=-\chi_{\Sigma}$ as $\varphi_{\Sigma}$ .

### 6.3 Entropies: Island and no-island phases

Now we turn to the problem of computing entropies using the RT formula in the background of the hyperbolic AdS3 black hole coupled to the AdS2 brane with JT gravity. Specifically, we wish to compute the entropy of the region $\mathbf{R}$ complementary to belts centered on the defects, as described at the end of subsection 6.2. In the island and no-island phases the RT formula equates the entropy to:

$$ \displaystyle\left[\frac{A(\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\text{bulk}}}+\phi_{\mathrm{QES}}\right]_{\mathrm{isl.}}\ \ ,\ \ \left[\frac{A(\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\text{bulk}}}\right]_{\cancel{\mathrm{isl.}}}. $$

The RT variational problem instructs us to consider extremal co-dimension two surfaces $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ in the bulk, which in AdS3 are simply geodesics. Although we are primarily concerned with evolution in Rindler time, the boundaries of the entangling surface are simply four points; these can always be simultaneously placed on a surface of constant global time. This property, not present in higher dimensions, allows us to simplify the analysis by using global coordinates4343 43 The fact that the endpoints reside at constant global time, together with the conservation of the charge associated with the global time Killing vector (obtained by dotting with the RT tangent) implies that the RT surfaces themselves must reside on constant global time slices. as seen below.

Now just as in higher dimensions, the minimization procedure yields two competing phases. At early times, the minimal surfaces cross the Rindler horizon avoiding the brane and the entropy is given purely by the bulk length of the RT surface, as in the second of the expressions (145). This length stretches with Rindler time and leads to a growing entropy. At late times the RT surfaces go across the brane instead, leading to an island where the contribution of the dilaton becomes important, as shown in the first of the expressions (145). As in the rest of the paper, we restrict to the regime of small brane angle $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ .

We begin by considering geodesics and their lengths in global coordinates. As is well known, a convenient way to parametrize the RT surfaces on constant global time $\tilde{\tau}$ is by using two anchoring points $\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2}$ , where geodesics are given by

$$ \displaystyle\sin(\tilde{r})\cos\left(\varphi-\frac{\varphi_{1}+\varphi_{2}}{2}\right)= \displaystyle\cos\left(\frac{\varphi_{2}-\varphi_{1}}{2}\right)\,. $$

such that the curves hit the boundary $\tilde{r}\to\pi/2$ at $\varphi_{1}$ and $\varphi_{2}$ . The area (length in $d=2$ ) of an RT surface with this trajectory is given by

$$ \displaystyle A= \displaystyle L\sum_{i\in\{1,2\}}\tanh^{-1}\left[\csc\left(\frac{\Delta\varphi}{2}\right)\sqrt{-\cos\left(\frac{\Delta\varphi}{2}+\tilde{r}_{i}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\Delta\varphi}{2}-\tilde{r}_{i}\right)}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle L\log\left[\frac{4\sin^{2}\left(\Delta\varphi/2\right)}{\epsilon_{1}\epsilon_{2}}\right]-\frac{L}{12}\left(1+3\cot^{2}\frac{\Delta\varphi}{2}\right)(\epsilon_{1}^{2}+\epsilon_{2}^{2})+O(\epsilon_{1}^{4})+O(\epsilon_{2}^{4})\,, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\Delta\varphi= \displaystyle|\varphi_{1}-\varphi_{2}|, \displaystyle\epsilon_{i}=\frac{\pi}{2}-\tilde{r}_{i}\qquad(i\in\{1,2\}) $$

are respectively the opening angle of the RT surface and the UV cutoffs (in the global radial coordinate) at which the area integral is terminated, see figure 23.

The leading order term in eq. (148) corresponds to the standard entanglement entropy formula of an interval on the circle [115, 17] (but allowing now for two different UV cutoffs). We have also included the next-to-leading order terms as these will be important for computing corrections to entropy formulas on the brane.

Now as usual, one must appropriately regularize the areas of the RT surfaces. As explained above, we place the cutoff surface at a large holographic radius $r=r_{\mathrm{UV}}$ in the Rindler radial coordinate. In terms of global coordinates, this describes the surface

$$ \displaystyle\sin^{2}(\tilde{\tau}) \displaystyle=\left(\sin\tilde{r}\cos\varphi\right)^{2}-(r_{\mathrm{UV}}^{2}-1)\cos^{2}(\tilde{r})\ . $$

Expanding to leading order in $r_{\mathrm{UV}}$ , one finds that the UV cutoff is associated with a length in eq. (149) given by

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon_{1}=\frac{1}{r_{\mathrm{UV}}}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\cosh(2\tau)+\cosh(2\chi)}}+O(r_{\mathrm{UV}}^{-3})\ . $$

where we have used eq. (144). Here and below, we shall use $\epsilon_{1}$ to denote the cutoff at the end-point of the RT surface at the asymptotic boundary; $\epsilon_{2}$ , on the other hand, will either be a cutoff at the asymptotic boundary or due to the brane, depending on whether we are in the no-island or island phase. Note that although the entropies diverge with the regulator $r_{\mathrm{UV}}$ , these contributions will cancel once we consider the difference between the island and no island phases, as seen below.

Equipped with this, we can now compute the generalized entropy in the two phases and reproduce the Page curve found in [2].

#### No-island phase.

We begin with the no-island phase. Here once again due to the simplicity of AdS3, the minimal surfaces lie on constant global time slices. The RT surface consists of two pieces, one connected piece on either side of the brane with trajectory given by eq. (146) where $\varphi_{1}=-\varphi_{\Sigma}$ and $\varphi_{2}=-\pi+\varphi_{\Sigma}$ (recall the definition of $\varphi_{\Sigma}$ below eq. (144)). The total RT length is given by double eq. (148) (due to the two pieces) with both cutoffs $\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}$ given by eq. (151). Substituting this into eq. (148) with $\Delta\varphi=\pi-2\varphi_{\Sigma}$ and using eq. (144), the associated entanglement entropy in the no-island phase is

$$ \displaystyle\left[\frac{A(\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\text{bulk}}}\right]_{\cancel{\mathrm{isl.}}} \displaystyle=\frac{L}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\log\left(2r_{\mathrm{UV}}\cosh\tau\right) \displaystyle=\frac{2c}{3}\log\left[\frac{\beta}{\pi\delta}\cosh\left(\frac{2\pi t}{\beta}\right)\right], $$

where we used the Brown-Henneaux central charge

$$ \displaystyle c=\frac{3L}{2G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}. $$

In the second line of eq. (152), we have expressed the answer in terms of the dimensionful time $t$ , as in eq. (139) (see also below eq. (16)) and the short-distance cutoff in the boundary CFT

$$ \displaystyle\delta=\frac{\beta}{2\pi\,r_{\mathrm{UV}}} $$

in the $y^{\pm}$ coordinates on the boundary4444 44 To be precise, eq. (152) computes the entropy of $\mathbf{R}$ in a CFT with metric $-dy^{+}dy^{-}$ and short distance cutoff $\delta$ — here, $\delta$ is both the proper distance cutoff and the cutoff in $y^{\pm}$ . We may equivalently take the CFT metric to be the induced metric $-\left(\frac{L}{\delta}\right)^{2}dy^{+}dy^{-}$ , in eq. (142), with coordinate cutoff $\delta$ in $y^{\pm}$ , corresponding to a proper distance cutoff $L$ as measured by the induced metric. . Eq. (152) matches the entropy from eq. (29) of [2], accounting for the fact that here the central charge is doubled since we include the regions on both sides of the brane4545 45 There is a typo in eq. (29) of [2]: inside the logarithm, it should be $\beta/\pi$ rather than $\pi/\beta$ . The UV cutoff $\delta$ is also hidden. The full answer is obtained by applying the conformal transformation $\displaystyle w^{\pm}=$ $\displaystyle\tanh\left(\frac{\pi y_{R}^{\pm}}{\beta}\right)=-\coth\left(\frac{\pi y_{L}^{\pm}}{\beta}\right)$ (155) (mapping the vacuum to a TFD) to the entropy formula $\displaystyle S[-dw^{+}dw^{-},\delta]=$ $\displaystyle\frac{c}{6}\log\left[-\frac{(w_{R}^{+}-w_{L}^{+})(w_{R}^{-}-w_{L}^{-})}{\delta^{2}}\right]$ (156) $\displaystyle\begin{split}\to S[-dy^{+}dy^{-},\delta]=&S[-dw^{+}dw^{-},\delta]-\frac{c}{12}\log(\partial_{y_{R}^{+}}w_{R}^{+}\partial_{y_{R}^{-}}w_{R}^{-}\partial_{y_{L}^{+}}w_{L}^{+}\partial_{y_{L}^{-}}w_{L}^{-}),\end{split}$ (157) where $y_{R}^{\pm}=t\pm b$ and $y_{L}^{\pm}=t\mp b$ are the entangling surfaces on the $R$ and $L$ sides respectively. We have used the notation $S[ds^{2},\delta]$ to denote entropy in a CFT living in $ds^{2}$ with proper distance cutoff $\delta$ as measured by $ds^{2}$ . Eq. (157) gives the length of the piece of the RT surface to one side of the brane; eq. (152) is then exactly double eq. (157). . For times much larger than the thermal scale,

$$ \displaystyle\left[\frac{A(\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\text{bulk}}}\right]_{\cancel{\mathrm{isl.}}}= \displaystyle\frac{2c}{3}\left[\log\left(\frac{\beta}{2\pi\delta}\right)+\frac{2\pi t}{\beta}\right]+O\left(ce^{-4\pi t/\beta}\right)\ , $$

which corresponds to the linear growth predicted by Hawking.

#### Island phase.

Let us next consider the island phase. As explained in section 2, since translations in Rindler time are an isometry, we can use this symmetry to bring the problem to the $\tilde{\tau}=0=\tau$ slice. Notice that this is also a symmetry of the dilaton profile as is clear from eq. (140).

We will leave point 1 anchored on the cutoff surface near the asymptotic boundary at global coordinate $\varphi_{1}=-\varphi_{\Sigma}$ , as in the no-island phase. But, the RT surface will now intersect the brane at its other endpoint. Here it is important to distinguish between two different angles appearing in the island calculation – see figure 23. First, $\varphi_{2}$ (together with $\varphi_{1}$ ) characterize the trajectory of the RT surface, as in eq. (146), such that the trajectory, when maximally extended (even behind the brane), reaches the asymptotic boundary at $\varphi_{1}$ and $\varphi_{2}$ . The opening angle $\Delta\varphi$ appearing in eq. (148) is defined in terms of $\varphi_{1}$ and $\varphi_{2}$ as per eq. (149). Second, there is the global angular coordinate $\varphi=\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}}$ of the QES where the RT surface intersects the brane. In the limit of vanishing brane angle $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\to 0$ , $\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}}\to\varphi_{2}$ but, at finite $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ , $\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}}\neq\varphi_{2}$ .

While $\epsilon_{1}$ is still given by eq. (151), the regulator $\epsilon_{2}$ is now provided by the brane position and is given by

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon_{2}= \displaystyle\tan^{-1}\left[\tan(\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}})\sin(\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}})\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\sin(\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}})+\frac{\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{3}}{3}\sin(\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}})\cos^{2}(\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}})+O(\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{5})\,, $$

which we use below perturbatively in the regime of $\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\ll 1$ . From eq. (148), the area of the RT surface (including the pieces to either side of the brane and to either side of the horizon) is given in terms of $\varphi_{\Sigma}$ and $\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}}$ by

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\left[\frac{A(\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\text{bulk}}}\right]_{\mathrm{isl.}}=&\frac{L}{G_{\text{bulk}}}\log\left[\frac{4}{\epsilon_{1}\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}\frac{\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\varphi_{\Sigma}+\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}}}{2}\right)}{\sin(\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}})}\right]\\
&+\frac{L\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}{G_{\text{bulk}}}\left[-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{\sin^{2}\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}}}{4\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\varphi_{\Sigma}+\varphi_{\mathrm{QES}}}{2}\right)}\right]+O\left(\frac{L\theta_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{4}}{G_{\text{bulk}}}\right)\,.\end{split} $$

We can also write this in terms of the $y^{\pm}$ coordinates of [2], reviewed around eqs. (138) and (142) (see also footnote 42). ### 6.4 Page curve

Collecting together the results of the previous subsection, we have two phases. At early times, we have the no-island phase, with generalized entropy given by eq. (152). Over time, this entropy grows at a rate proportional to the temperature $1/\beta$ and the number $c$ of matter degrees of freedom participating in Hawking radiation, as emphasized in eq. (158). This growth, however is capped off by an island phase, where quantum extremal surfaces on the brane just outside the black hole horizon surround an island, containing a portion of the black hole interior, now belonging to the entanglement wedge of the bath. In this latter phase, generalized entropy is given by the constant value written in eq. (170) which is dominated by double the Bekenstein-Hawking black hole entropy, as given in eq. (171). Viewing eq. (171) as the course-grained entropy for the two sides of the black hole, this is precisely the expected maximal entropy of the system.

To find the Page time $\tau_{P}=2\pi t_{P}/\beta$ marking the transition between the two phases, we equate the corresponding generalized entropies given in eqs. (158) and (170):

$$ \displaystyle\tau_{P}=\frac{2\pi t_{P}}{\beta} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{3}{c}\left(\hat{\phi}_{0}+\frac{2\pi\phi_{r}}{\beta}\right)+\log(2)+\frac{2\pi b}{\beta}-\frac{\tilde{\delta}^{2}}{4\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}^{2}}\left(1-e^{-\frac{4\pi b}{\beta}}\right)-\frac{c\beta e^{-\frac{4\pi b}{\beta}}}{12\pi\phi_{r}} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\quad+O\left({\tilde{\delta}^{4}}/{\ell_{\textrm{\tiny JT}}^{4}}\right)+O\left({c^{2}\beta^{2}}/{\phi_{r}^{2}}\right)\,. $$

Overall, we recover a Page curve, with entropy growing linearly in a no-island phase up to the Page time, and saturating to a constant maximal value in an island phase after the Page time.
